source.title: Feature Drift: How Fine-Tuning Repurposes Representations in LLMs
source.authors: Andrey V. Galichin; Anton Korznikov; Alexey Dontsov; Oleg Y. Rogov; Elena Tutubalina; I. Oseledets

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether SAE features transfer across base and chat models and refines the stable-feature account by measuring systematic activation drift and testing selected features causally.
record.gate_note: Included the study's own SAE-transfer, feature-drift, refusal-direction reconstruction, and causal-intervention results. Cited findings from other work and SAE hyperparameters are not results of this study. Per-model and per-layer values shown only graphically are not extracted individually; the text reports aggregate ranges and degradation figures.
record.test_reason: The study mainly uses SAEs as a tool to study fine-tuning. Two of its results still bear on V5 in a new setting. First, it measures how well a base-model SAE dictionary reconstructs chat-model activations (stability of dictionary units across fine-tuning). Second, it shows that a known causal direction (refusal) is only partly reconstructed by SAE features (completeness). The refusal-mediation interventions and drift metrics concern fine-tuning mechanics, not any superposition version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that instruction tuning shifts when existing base-SAE features activate rather than creating new ones. They report 7-9% FVU transfer degradation, show drifted features causally mediate refusal, and call this a more complete though not exhaustive account.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses TopK SAEs to measure transfer and feature activation drift in fine-tuned LLMs, then uses activation-direction reconstruction and interventions. It does not test the original toy-network superposition setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Model family affects transfer degradation: Qwen2.5 shows minimal degradation. The study also reports results by early, middle, and late layers, but gives aggregate metric ranges in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: About 13-17% of tokens have base/chat activation cosine below 0.9. On these tokens ER is 0.3-0.7 and IR is 0.1-0.5, meaning the same dictionary features activate differently after fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning reallocates which existing SAE features activate (feature drift) rather than creating new features.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating directions built from chat-selected SAE features drops safety score from 1.0 to about 0.1. Adding them induces about 50% refusal. Base-selected features have weaker effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Drifted pre-existing SAE features causally mediate refusal in chat models.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2026
record.problems: The causal case study is limited to Gemma-2-2B-IT and refusal. No uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported in the text. The authors note that chat SAEs were trained on 0.5B tokens versus 2B for base SAEs, and that refusal-feature selection achieves cosine similarity 0.51 at k=64.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model/per-layer FVU and ER/IR values in Figures 1 and 3 were not entered separately because the text gives only plotted values for those breakdowns; the reported aggregate changes and ranges are included in R1-R7. Table 1 values for k=1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 are included in R8-R21.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transition, or geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity analysis.
No analysis of the origins of polysemanticity.
SAEs are assumed as the tool. No test of whether features spread across neurons, and no absolute evidence of sparse-feature recoverability beyond plotted FVU.
Canonicity across SAE sizes or seeds, and full-dictionary completeness, are not tested. Stability is tested only across base-to-chat fine-tuning.
Dimensionality of features is not examined.

missing.what: Per-model, per-layer absolute FVU values for base and chat SAEs (roughly 0.05-0.35 by plot). Needed to judge reconstruction quality and transfer by model.
Fraction of tokens with base/chat cosine below 0.9 (13.0%, 17.1%, 12.7% median by layer).

record.verdict_notes: The study is primarily T4-like: it treats SAEs as a tool for model diffing. Only the transfer results and the refusal-direction completeness bear on V5. The reader's V4 links were dropped because the study assumes, rather than tests, that LLMs contain SAE-recoverable features. The k-sweep rows and the intervention rows describe the study's own method, not version measures. Chat SAEs used 0.5B tokens vs 2B for base SAEs, which affects the R4 comparison. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition geometry, feature sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemantic neurons result from capacity competition or feature importance.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The study does not measure features spread across neurons; it tests SAE reconstruction and selected SAE-feature interventions in the reported models and settings.
It does not establish whether SAE features are complete or canonical across models, behaviors, layers, or training stages.
Whether represented features are inherently one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: All tested model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured SAE fraction of variance unexplained (FVU) when base-data-trained SAEs reconstructed base-model activations on base data versus base-model activations on chat data.
rows.value: B-LLM + C-Data incurred approximately 5% increase in FVU
rows.note: Aggregate result across tested models and layer depths; the change is a degradation, although the authors describe transfer performance as strong.
rows.check: Measures dictionary transfer under a data shift (base model, chat data), not evidence that LLMs contain sparse features. Drop V4. About 5% FVU increase means the dictionary holds with some loss.

rows.subject: All tested model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the additional FVU change when transferring from base-model to chat-model activations, with chat data.
rows.value: The subsequent shift to C-LLM + C-Data added another 2-3%
rows.note: Aggregate result; this is additional reconstruction degradation.
rows.check: Additional 2-3% FVU from the base-to-chat model shift. Bears on dictionary stability across fine-tuning, not V4.

rows.subject: All tested model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared base SAE transfer to chat-model activations on chat data against the base-data/base-model setting.
rows.value: 7-8% performance degradation on chat models with chat data
rows.note: Aggregate result across the tested models; authors characterize transferred reconstruction as strong despite the degradation.
rows.check: Total 7-8% degradation. The base dictionary largely but not fully carries over. Drop V4.

rows.subject: All tested model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared transferred base SAE reconstruction with SAEs trained on chat models and chat data.
rows.measure: FVU degradation relative to chat SAE
rows.note: Aggregate comparison; the study says chat SAEs outperform transferred base SAEs.
rows.check: Chat-trained SAEs beat transferred base SAEs by about 9%, despite 4x fewer training tokens, so the base dictionary is not canonical for chat models. Drop V4.

rows.subject: All tested model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE reconstruction of chat activations with the base activation as a reference on filtered token pairs.
rows.value: ER ranges from 0.3 to 0.7; ER < 1.0 indicates the SAE captures chat-specific patterns beyond what base activations preserve
rows.note: Aggregate range reported across models and layer depths.
rows.check: The Explained Ratio compares SAE error with base-vs-chat divergence on filtered tokens. It is a drift metric, not a measure of dictionary completeness or stability.

rows.subject: All tested model families (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared active SAE features on paired base and chat representations.
rows.baseline: Feature-set overlap between base and chat representations
rows.note: The authors interpret the low overlap, together with modest reconstruction degradation, as systematic feature reallocation.
rows.check: The Intersection Ratio measures which features activate across paired activations (activation drift), not whether the features themselves are stable or canonical.

relation.reason: The study directly evaluates dictionary transfer across base/chat models and data, providing evidence about V5 stability and coverage beyond using SAEs as an analysis tool.

tranche.reason: The transfer results qualify V5: base dictionaries retain substantial reconstruction ability but incur measurable degradation and underperform chat-trained dictionaries. T5 covers results showing that a version is partial or needs qualification.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Base/chat SAE training budgets differ (2B versus 0.5B tokens); transfer reconstruction does not independently establish canonical units or isolate preference/RL and reasoning training stages.
